library(tidyverse)
library(ebirdst)
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(tidyterra)

# `terra` and `tidyr` both export `extract`; be explicit below where it matters.

theme_set(
  theme_minimal() +

## Overview

[eBird Status and Trends](https://science.ebird.org/en/status-and-trends)
provides modeled estimates of species distribution, relative abundance, and
population trend, derived from eBird checklists and remotely sensed habitat
covariates. Unlike the raw eBird observations used elsewhere in this package
(`klamath_ebird`), these are **effort-corrected model predictions** on a
regular grid, which makes them comparable across space rather than a
reflection of where birders happened to go.

This document pulls two distinct products and clips both to the Klamath
Basin boundary (`rivermile::klamath_hucs`):

1.  **Status** — seasonal relative abundance rasters (3 km resolution).
2.  **Trends** — modeled percent-per-year change in relative abundance
    (~27 km resolution), for 2012-2022.

```{r versions}
ebirdst_version()
```

Note that the status and trends products are on **different release
cycles** — the status estimates and the trends estimates are not from the
same model year, so they should not be described as a single vintage.

### Access key

Status and Trends data require a free access key, requested at
<https://ebird.org/st/request>. The key is a secret and should never be
typed into a chunk, script, or anything that gets committed. Run this once,
directly in the R console (not in this document):

```r
ebirdst::set_ebirdst_access_key("your-key-here")
```

That call writes `EBIRDST_KEY` into `~/.Renviron`, outside the project
directory. From then on every R session — including this document — picks
the key up automatically from the environment, so nothing in this file ever
needs to reference it directly. (The console command itself still lands in
your R history, so if that's a concern, edit `~/.Renviron` directly instead
of using the helper.)

## Study area

`rivermile::klamath_hucs` holds the 12 HUC8 subbasins that make up the
Klamath Basin. Both the dissolved outline (for clipping) and the individual
subbasins (for summarizing) are used below.

```{r study-area}
klamath_hucs <- rivermile::klamath_hucs
klamath_outline <- st_union(klamath_hucs)

glimpse(klamath_hucs)
```

Status estimates are also summarized by wildlife refuge, using
`rivermile::klamath_refuges` with the same 0.5-mile buffer and `site`
naming as `data-raw/bird_data_synthesis.Rmd` uses to build the `area`
column in `klamath_ebird` and `piscivorous_waterbirds`. Matching that
convention here means a status/trends value for, say, "Tule Lake" refers to
exactly the same boundary as the eBird observation and RTR colony data
elsewhere in this package, so the three can be compared directly.

```{r study-area-refuges}
refuge_buffer_dist <- units::set_units(0.5, "mi")

klamath_refuges <- rivermile::klamath_refuges |>
  mutate(
    site = case_when(
      str_detect(orgname, "bear valley")   ~ "Bear Valley",
      str_detect(orgname, "clear lake")    ~ "Clear Lake",
      str_detect(orgname, "klamath marsh") ~ "Klamath Marsh",
      str_detect(orgname, "lower klamath") ~ "Lower Klamath - Sheepy",
      str_detect(orgname, "tule lake")     ~ "Tule Lake",
      str_detect(orgname, "upper klamath") ~ "Upper Klamath Lake"
    )
  ) |>
  select(site, orgname) |>
  st_buffer(dist = refuge_buffer_dist)

glimpse(klamath_refuges)
```

Both Status and Trends products are distributed on global equal-area grids,
but **not the same one** — status rasters are Equal Earth
(EPSG:8857) while the trends grid is sinusoidal. Rather than hard-coding
either, the boundary is reprojected to whatever CRS the downloaded product
reports. Reprojecting the *vector* rather than the raster matters: warping
the raster would resample the estimates and distort the equal-area cells
that the abundance values are defined on.

## Species

The focal species here are the three tracked by the multispecies subgroup.
`ebirdst_runs` is the authoritative list of what is modeled, including
whether a species has trends estimates at all.

```{r species}
focal_species <- c("Cinnamon Teal", "Eared Grebe", "White-faced Ibis")

focal_runs <- ebirdst_runs |>
  filter(common_name %in% focal_species) |>
  select(
    common_name, species_code, is_resident,
    breeding_quality, nonbreeding_quality,
    has_trends, trends_season, trends_start_year, trends_end_year
  )

knitr::kable(focal_runs, caption = "Status and Trends model coverage for the focal species")
```

Two things to note before going further:

-   **Eared Grebe has no trends estimates** (`has_trends = FALSE`), so it
    appears in the status section but drops out of the trends section. Any
    species list used here should be filtered on `has_trends` rather than
    assumed complete.
-   Model quality is rated per season on a 0-3 scale. These ratings should
    be checked before interpreting a seasonal surface; a low rating means
    the model was poorly validated for that season.

## Status: seasonal relative abundance

These surfaces come from an ensemble of decision trees trained on eBird
checklists, each paired with satellite-derived land cover and other
environmental covariates at that checklist's location and date. The model
is calibrated to account for variation in observer effort, time of day, and
search duration, so that differences across the resulting surface reflect
differences in the birds rather than differences in who happened to go
looking. Predictions are made weekly across a regular global grid and then
averaged into the seasonal layers pulled below.

Downloads are cached in `ebirdst_data_dir()` and skipped if already
present, so this chunk is safe to re-run. The 3 km products are sizeable
per species — pass `dry_run = TRUE` to list the files first, or step down to
`"9km"` / `"27km"` if bandwidth is a concern.

```{r status-download}
status_resolution <- "3km"

walk(focal_species, \(sp) ebirdst_download_status(sp, download_abundance = TRUE))
```

`crop()` on these global rasters reads only the windowed region, so clipping
to the basin is cheap despite the global extent.

```{r status-clip}
#' Load a species' seasonal abundance and clip it to the Klamath Basin
clip_status_to_klamath <- function(species, resolution = status_resolution) {
  r <- load_raster(
    species,
    product    = "abundance",
    period     = "seasonal",
    metric     = "mean",
    resolution = resolution
  )

  # Reproject the boundary into the raster's own CRS, not the reverse.
  boundary <- st_transform(klamath_outline, terra::crs(r)) |> vect()

  r |>
    terra::crop(boundary) |>
    terra::mask(boundary)
}

status_klamath <- set_names(focal_species) |> map(clip_status_to_klamath)

# Seasonal layers differ by species (migrants get four seasons, residents
# one), so report what each actually returned.
map(status_klamath, names)
```

```{r status-maps, fig.height=8}
display_crs <- "EPSG:32610"
display_buffer <- units::set_units(15, "km")

plot_status <- function(species, resolution = status_resolution) {
  r <- load_raster(
    species,
    product    = "abundance",
    period     = "seasonal",
    metric     = "mean",
    resolution = resolution
  )

  # Loose crop, still in the native CRS, just to keep the reprojection cheap.
  wide_boundary <- st_buffer(klamath_outline, display_buffer) |>
    st_transform(terra::crs(r)) |>
    vect()
  r_wide <- terra::crop(r, wide_boundary)

  # Reproject before the tight crop - see note above.
  r_disp <- terra::project(r_wide, display_crs, method = "bilinear")

  # Only now compute the tight boundary, directly in the display CRS.
  tight_boundary <- st_transform(klamath_outline, display_crs) |> vect()
  r_disp <- r_disp |> terra::crop(tight_boundary) |> terra::mask(tight_boundary)

  ggplot() +
    geom_spatraster(data = r_disp) +
    geom_sf(data = st_transform(klamath_hucs, display_crs),
            fill = NA, color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.25) +
    facet_wrap(~ lyr) +
    scale_fill_gradientn(
      colours = ebirdst_palettes(20, type = "weekly"),
      na.value = "transparent",
      name = "Relative\nabundance"
    ) +
    labs(
      title = species,
      subtitle = paste0("Seasonal mean relative abundance, ", status_resolution,
                        " resolution, clipped to the Klamath Basin")
    ) +
    theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
}

walk(focal_species, \(sp) print(plot_status(sp)))
```

### What `mean_abundance` means

Each raster cell's own value — before any summarizing — is the *relative
abundance* eBird Status defines it: the expected count of the species on a
standardized 2 km, 1 hour Traveling Count by an expert eBird observer,
at the optimal time of day and under optimal conditions to detect that
species, computed as the modeled probability of occurrence times the
expected count given occurrence. The seasonal layers used throughout this
document are the cell-wise *mean* of that quantity across the weeks in a
season. `mean_abundance` below is a further spatial mean of those
already-averaged cells, taken over every 3 km cell whose centre falls
inside a subbasin or refuge polygon.

So `mean_abundance` is a mean of means, on a relative, checklist-referenced
scale — **not** a density, a population estimate, or a count of birds. It
is only meaningful as a comparison: across seasons for one place, across
places for one species, or across species where their models used the same
standardized-checklist definition. It is *not* an absolute number of birds
that can be summed to a population total.

Summarizing each seasonal surface by subbasin, and separately by refuge, and
stacking both into a single `ebird_status` table gives one object that
joins to the rest of the package two ways: on `huc8` (matching
`rivermile::klamath_hucs`) for subbasin rows, and on `area` (matching
`klamath_ebird$area` and `piscivorous_waterbirds$area`) for refuge rows.
The two geographies don't nest — a refuge isn't contained in one subbasin,
and vice versa — so rather than force them into one geometry, each row
carries a `geography_type` column (`"huc8"` or `"refuge"`) and only the
relevant id columns are populated; the other geography's id columns are
`NA` on that row.

```{r ebird-status}
#' Zonal mean of a status raster within each feature of a polygon layer
summarise_by_polygon <- function(r, species, polygons, id_cols) {
  polygons_prj <- st_transform(polygons, terra::crs(r))

  terra::extract(r, vect(polygons_prj), fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE, ID = FALSE) |>
    as_tibble() |>
    bind_cols(st_drop_geometry(polygons_prj) |> select(all_of(id_cols))) |>
    pivot_longer(
      -all_of(id_cols),
      names_to  = "season",
      values_to = "mean_abundance"
    ) |>
    mutate(common_name = species, .before = everything()) |>
    # Cells can be entirely NA inside a feature (outside the modeled range).
    mutate(mean_abundance = if_else(is.nan(mean_abundance), NA_real_, mean_abundance))
}

status_by_huc <- imap(
  status_klamath,
  \(r, sp) summarise_by_polygon(r, sp, klamath_hucs, c("huc8", "name"))
) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  transmute(
    common_name, geography_type = "huc8",
    huc8, name, area = NA_character_,
    season, mean_abundance
  )

status_by_refuge <- imap(
  status_klamath,
  \(r, sp) summarise_by_polygon(r, sp, klamath_refuges, c("site"))
) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  transmute(
    common_name, geography_type = "refuge",
    huc8 = NA_character_, name = NA_character_, area = site,
    season, mean_abundance
  )

ebird_status <- bind_rows(status_by_huc, status_by_refuge) |>
  glimpse()

usethis::use_data(ebird_status, overwrite = TRUE)
```

```{r status-tables}
ebird_status |>
  filter(geography_type == "huc8", !is.na(mean_abundance)) |>
  arrange(common_name, season, desc(mean_abundance)) |>
  select(-geography_type, -area) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4, caption = "Mean seasonal relative abundance by HUC8 subbasin")

ebird_status |>
  filter(geography_type == "refuge", !is.na(mean_abundance)) |>
  arrange(common_name, season, desc(mean_abundance)) |>
  select(-geography_type, -huc8, -name) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4, caption = "Mean seasonal relative abundance by wildlife refuge")
```

```{r status-huc-plot, fig.height=8}
status_pal <- c("Cinnamon Teal" = "#2a78d6", "Eared Grebe" = "#eb6834",
                "White-faced Ibis" = "#1baf7a")

ebird_status |>
  filter(geography_type == "huc8", !is.na(mean_abundance)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_abundance, y = fct_reorder(name, mean_abundance, .fun = max),
             fill = common_name)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(preserve = "single")) +
  facet_wrap(~ season, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = status_pal, name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title = "Which subbasins hold the most predicted abundance",
    x = "Mean relative abundance", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r status-refuge-plot, fig.height=6}
ebird_status |>
  filter(geography_type == "refuge", !is.na(mean_abundance)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_abundance, y = fct_reorder(area, mean_abundance, .fun = max),
             fill = common_name)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(preserve = "single")) +
  facet_wrap(~ season, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = status_pal, name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title = "Which refuges hold the most predicted abundance",
    subtitle = "Same six refuges used for `area` in klamath_ebird and piscivorous_waterbirds",
    x = "Mean relative abundance", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Trends: percent change per year

Trends are estimated differently from status. Rather than modeling absolute
abundance in a single year, the trends model finds pairs of checklists that
are close in location and similar in habitat and survey effort but taken in
different years, and asks how relative abundance differed between the two
years of each pair. Averaging that year-over-year change across many such
pairs within a grid cell yields a percent-per-year trend for the cell, along
with a confidence interval. Because it relies on paired comparisons rather
than a single-year surface, this product is modeled on a coarser (~27 km)
grid than status, and only for the 2012-2022 breeding season here. Trend
estimates arrive as a data frame of grid cell centres with
longitude/latitude in EPSG:4326, so the clip is a spatial filter of points
rather than a raster mask.

```{r trends-download}
trends_species <- focal_runs |>
  filter(has_trends) |>
  pull(common_name)

trends_species

walk(trends_species, ebirdst_download_trends)
```

```{r trends-clip}
trends_raw <- set_names(trends_species) |>
  map(\(sp) load_trends(sp)) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "common_name")

# Cell centres are lon/lat, so filter in 4326 against the basin outline.
trends_sf <- trends_raw |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)

trends_klamath <- trends_sf |>
  st_filter(st_transform(klamath_outline, 4326), .predicate = st_intersects)

# How many 27 km cells actually fall inside the basin?
trends_klamath |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(common_name, season, name = "n_cells")
```

```{r trends-map, fig.height=6}
# ebirdst's own trends palette runs red (decline) -> white (no change) ->
# blue (increase). Keep that direction: it is the convention every published
# Status and Trends map uses, and flipping it would invert the reading.
trends_pal <- ebirdst_palettes(3, type = "trends")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = st_transform(klamath_hucs, 4326), fill = "grey94", color = "grey70",
          linewidth = 0.25) +
  # shape 21 keeps near-zero (near-white) cells visible against the basin.
  geom_sf(data = trends_klamath, aes(fill = abd_ppy),
          shape = 21, color = "grey35", stroke = 0.3, size = 3.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ common_name) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = trends_pal[1], mid = trends_pal[2], high = trends_pal[3],
    midpoint = 0,
    name = "% change\nper year"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Modeled population trend within the Klamath Basin",
    subtitle = "Percent change per year in breeding-season relative abundance, 2012-2022",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```

A diverging scale centred on zero is used deliberately: the quantity has a
meaningful neutral point (no change), and the two arms read as opposite
directions — **red is decline, blue is increase**, following eBird's own
convention. Cell-level estimates carry wide confidence intervals, so the
summary below reports them rather than the point estimate alone.

```{r trends-summary}
trends_klamath |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(
    n_cells         = n(),
    median_ppy      = median(abd_ppy),
    mean_ppy        = mean(abd_ppy),
    median_ppy_low  = median(abd_ppy_lower),
    median_ppy_high = median(abd_ppy_upper),
    cells_declining = sum(abd_ppy < 0),
    .by = c(common_name, season)
  ) |>
  arrange(median_ppy) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Trend summary for cells intersecting the Klamath Basin")
```

Assigning trend cells to individual subbasins is possible but marginal at
this resolution: a single 27 km cell is comparable in size to the smaller
HUC8s, so a per-subbasin trend would mostly reflect which cell centre landed
where. Basin-wide summaries are the appropriate grain for this product.

## Caveats

-   **Model output, not observation.** These are predictions from a model
    fit to eBird data. They are effort-corrected, which is precisely why
    they are useful alongside `klamath_ebird`, but they inherit the
    assumptions of the underlying model.
-   **Check seasonal quality ratings.** A surface for a season rated 0-1
    should not be interpreted; see the species table above.
-   **Resolution mismatch.** Status is clipped at 3 km, trends at ~27 km.
    The two are not directly comparable cell-for-cell, and the basin
    contains relatively few trend cells.
-   **Edge effects.** Clipping to a watershed or refuge boundary cuts
    through modeled surfaces that are continuous across it. Cells
    straddling the boundary are included whole by `mask()` (based on cell
    centre), so edge values partly describe habitat just outside the
    polygon. This matters far more for `status_by_refuge` than
    `status_by_huc`: refuges are small relative to the 3 km grid — Bear
    Valley (~17 km²) is only about 2 cells, versus 10-24 cells for the
    other five refuges — so a refuge-level mean, especially Bear Valley's,
    rests on very little spatial averaging and should be read as
    indicative rather than precise.
-   **Trends are breeding-season only** for these species, so they say
    nothing about the migratory and wintering periods that the status
    surfaces do cover.

## Citation

Data products must be cited; `ebirdst` bundles the current citation.

```{r citation, eval=FALSE}
citation("ebirdst")
```
